summary: Standing some 5.6 metres high on the shore of Lough Neagh, the Ardboe cross is the tallest high cross in Northern Ireland and one of the most completely carved, with twenty-two panels of Old and New Testament scenes. The photograph shows the east face, whose head is crowded with small figures around the central Christ of the Second Coming and the Last Judgment; the opposite face of the head carries the Passion and the Crucifixion. Although weathering has softened the carving, the cross still reads as a complete sermon in stone, leading the eye from the stories of Israel up to Christ the Judge.
facts: The east face is given over mainly to Old Testament scenes (Adam and Eve, the Sacrifice of Isaac, Daniel in the lions' den, the Three Hebrews in the furnace), while the west face shows the Adoration of the Magi, the Wedding at Cana, the Multiplication of the Loaves and Christ's Entry into Jerusalem, and the north side the early life of Christ including his Baptism.

The cross stands at the site of a monastery traditionally founded by St Colman around 590; the head is damaged, but the cross is thought to be the only one in Northern Ireland to remain largely complete and original.
notes: Scene programme from the Wikipedia article; in this general view the Last Judgment on the head is recognisable as a central figure among crowded rows of small figures, but individual details are worn. Dated to the 10th century by most accounts, with some suggesting the 9th.

summary: The head of the high cross at Drumcliff, on the site of a monastery founded by St Columba, is carved with a standing figure of Christ at the crossing, usually identified as Christ in Glory, with small figures on the arms and a panel of Daniel below. The other face of the cross turns to the Gospel: the Arrest or Mocking of Christ between two soldiers and, higher up, the Crucifixion with Stephaton offering the vinegar and Longinus raising his spear. It is the only surviving high cross of its kind in County Sligo.
facts: The cross is said to bear the only known representation of the Virgin and Child on any Irish high cross, on the side of one arm.
Its scheme gives unusual prominence to the infancy of John the Baptist, a figure much honoured in the Columban monastic tradition.
High-relief animals, including a camel on one face and a lion on the other, stride across the shaft between the scriptural panels.
notes: Dating is uncertain: the Drumcliff Monastery article gives a tentative 9th or 10th century on artistic grounds, while the Drumcliff article dates the cross to c. 1100. The identification of the head figure as Christ in Glory follows the photographer's caption; many scenes on this cross are debated.

summary: Only the shaft of the Broken Cross survives, but its panels are among the clearest Gospel scenes on any Irish cross. At the foot of the east face Christ stands in the Jordan, shown as two streams springing from round sources, while figures on either side attend the Baptism; in the panel above, a row of figures has been read as the Wedding Feast at Cana, where Christ worked his first sign. Even broken, the cross speaks of the new life of baptism and of the abundance of Christ's gifts.
facts: Peter Harbison identified the panels of the east face, from the bottom, as the Baptism of Christ, the Marriage Feast at Cana and, higher up, the Healing at Bethesda and Christ with the Woman of Samaria.

The Broken Cross is one of several crosses in the monastic enclosure at Kells, the house associated with St Columba and the Book of Kells; it may once have been among the tallest of all Irish high crosses.

links.label: Image on Wikimedia Commons (with Harbison's identifications)

notes: Panel identifications follow Peter Harbison as quoted on the Commons file page; the Commons description also notes that the photographer questions the Bethesda reading, since one figure appears to hold a lyre. The cross is said to have been broken in the 17th century, possibly by Cromwellian troops, but this is not documented. Date not securely established.

summary: The South Cross at Clonmacnoise is covered almost entirely with bosses, spirals and interlace, but at the top of the shaft on its west face a single Christian scene is set: Christ crucified, in a long robe, with the sponge-bearer and the spear-bearer at his sides. Now displayed indoors in the visitor centre, the cross shows how early Irish sculptors placed the Crucifixion at the heart of an otherwise abstract decoration.
facts: This is the only Christian figure scene on the cross; many believe the South Cross was a partial inspiration for the later and more elaborate Cross of the Scriptures at the same monastery.
The original was moved into the visitor centre to protect it from the weather, and a replica stands on its old site at the southern end of the monastery's central area.
notes: The figures flanking Christ are identified as Stephaton and Longinus from their poses and the conventions of Irish crosses.

summary: This fragment of a free-standing Pictish cross from Monifieth opens with the Crucifixion: the lower part of Christ's long-robed body remains on the cross, flanked by two figures standing at his feet, while the upper part has broken away. Below, pairs of robed figures and men with drinking horns lead down to a seated harpist, a sequence that sets Christ's sacrifice above the life of the community.
facts: The stone was once built into the front of St Regulus' Church at Monifieth and may originally have stood at St Bride's Ring, Kingennie; it was given to the Museum of Antiquities in Edinburgh in 1870.
The seated harpist at the foot of the shaft resembles the harper on the Dupplin Cross; a second Monifieth fragment (Monifieth 5) also carried a Crucifixion with Christ broken off at the waist.
notes: Class III (no Pictish symbols). The precise date is not secure; the 9th–10th century range is an estimate for Pictish Class III sculpture of this kind.

summary: On the broken shaft of the Anglo-Saxon cross at Bradbourne, Christ hangs on the cross beneath the two discs of sun and moon, his arms outstretched along the cross-bar, while two smaller figures stand below at either side, the soldiers who bring the sponge and the spear. Weathered and patched together after being broken, it remains a moving early English image of the Crucifixion set up in the open churchyard for all to see.
facts: The cross was at some point smashed and has since been partially reconstructed in the churchyard of All Saints, a church site that goes back to Saxon times.
Sun and moon above the Cross recall the darkness at the Crucifixion and became a standard feature of early medieval Crucifixion images.
notes: Wikipedia describes it as an 8th-century depiction of the Crucifixion; other accounts place the cross in the early 9th century. The identification of the lower flanking figures as Stephaton and Longinus follows the usual convention.

summary: Over the doorway in the porch of the Anglo-Saxon church at Breamore, a large stone rood shows Christ on the cross between the Virgin Mary and St John, beneath the hand of God reaching down from a cloud. The figures were cut back flush with the wall, probably at the Reformation, so that what survives is chiefly their outline and traces of medieval painting around them; even so the composition of the Cross between the two mourners is still plain.
facts: St Mary's, Breamore, is an almost complete Anglo-Saxon church; an Old English inscription of the reign of Æthelred the Unready survives on the arch to its south porticus.
The roundel of the Lamb of God set below the rood is a later, 12th-century addition.
notes: Badly mutilated; the date is approximate and usually given as around 1000. The Reformation as the occasion of the defacement is the usual explanation, not a documented fact.

summary: This small limestone panel shows Christ crucified with a halo, between two angels above the cross-arm and two haloed mourners, usually taken to be the Virgin Mary and St John. Below them two figures raise the spear and the sponge on long shafts, and leafy scrolls spring up beside the foot of the cross. It is a distinct work from the larger 'Romsey Rood' on the outside wall of the abbey, and one of the most complete Anglo-Saxon Crucifixion carvings to survive in England.
facts: Romsey Abbey describes it as a low-relief carving of the Crucifixion on a block of limestone, probably of the 10th century, now framed by an altar consecrated in 2015.
King Edgar refounded (or founded) the nunnery at Romsey in 967 under the Rule of St Benedict, the period to which local tradition links the carving.
notes: Not the same work as the large external Romsey Rood already in the collection (wga:m/master/yunk_en/00cross). The figure identifications are inferred from the iconography; the date is given by the abbey as 'probably 10th century'.

summary: Inside a roundel bordered by flowers, this heavy silk shows the newborn Christ, swaddled in the manger, with the ox and the ass leaning over him; a haloed figure stands at the left and a large seated figure fills the right of the scene. The silk was used to wrap or cover one of the relics in the Sancta Sanctorum, the private chapel of the popes at the Lateran, and so survived the centuries in the dark of the papal treasury.
facts: It belongs with a companion silk of the same weave showing the Annunciation (Vatican inv. 61231); both were used in the Sancta Sanctorum and are now in the Vatican Museums.

The Sancta Sanctorum, first mentioned in the Liber Pontificalis under Pope Stephen III (768–772), served as the popes' private oratory; its main altar held a cypress-wood relic chest placed there by Pope Leo III (795–816).

links.label: Image on Wikimedia Commons (with museum label)

notes: Date and possible Syrian origin follow the Vatican Museums label quoted on Commons. The identities of the haloed standing figure and the seated figure (the Virgin, Joseph or a midwife) are not given on the label and are left open here.

summary: This silver box was made to hold the enamelled cross-reliquary of Pope Paschal I. On its lid a bearded, haloed Christ sits enthroned and blesses, holding a book, between St Peter with his cross-staff and St Paul with a codex, while two winged angels look on from roundels above and small figures are worked at the foot of the throne. Gilded against the silver ground, the lid presents Christ as Lord of the Church, guarded by the apostles of Rome.
facts: The case belongs to the enamelled cross of Paschal I (Vatican inv. 61881), one of the treasures kept in the Lateran chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum.
The Sancta Sanctorum acquired the enamelled cross commissioned by Paschal I (pope 817–824) among the relics added over time to the chapel's treasury.

links.label: Image on Wikimedia Commons (with museum label)

notes: The Vatican label (quoted on Commons) says only 'perhaps Rome, 9th century'; association with Paschal I's pontificate follows from its function as the case of his cross. The identifications of Christ, Peter and Paul rest on their attributes. The cross itself (cur:objects2-paschal-enamel-cross) and the separate silver cruciform case (cur:objects2-paschal-silver-cruciform-case) are already in the collection; this is a different object.

summary: This small wooden reliquary for a fragment of the True Cross has a cross-shaped cavity, around which are painted on gold the half-figure of Christ holding a book, the Virgin turned towards him with hands raised in prayer, two archangels, and full-length figures of Saints Paul and Peter, named in Greek. The Virgin's gesture of intercession towards her Son gives the little box the sense of a prayer gathered around the relic of the Cross.
facts: The inside of the sliding lid is painted with St John Chrysostom, and its outer face with a Crucifixion that is not visible in this photograph.
It came to the Vatican Museums from the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum at the Lateran.
